1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text: The patient is a 53-year-old man from Hunan whose chief complaint was "multiserosal effusions found for 1 year, chest tightness and shortness of breath for more than 3 months," and he was admitted to our hospital's Department of Respiratory Medicine in approximately 12 months after Day 0. On Day 0, he was hospitalized at a local hospital for cerebral hemorrhage. Chest CT showed a small amount of fibrosis and calcified lesions in the right upper lung, diffuse inflammation in both lungs, small bilateral pleural effusions, mildly enlarged cardiac silhouette, a small pericardial effusion, and a small amount of ascites. He underwent neuroendoscopic intracerebral hematoma evacuation under general anesthesia at the local hospital and was discharged after rehabilitation. In May, August, and approximately 9 months after Day 0, he was hospitalized three times in the Endocrinology Department of the local hospital for "elevated blood glucose found for 2 years, weakness and numbness of both lower extremities for several months." Imaging showed that the pleural, pericardial, and peritoneal effusions had gradually increased compared with before. Urinalysis showed occult blood 2+, glucose 3+, and protein 1+. Hypoproteinemia was present (total protein 57 g/L, albumin 30 g/L). Electromyography and nerve conduction studies suggested involvement of both motor and sensory nerves of the extremities. Pleural fluid results were borderline between exudate and transudate. Routine pleural fluid analysis: light yellow, total cell count 120×10^6/L, multinuclear cells 24%, mononuclear cells 75%, Rivalta test +; pleural fluid biochemistry: total protein 32.6 g/L, albumin 21.2 g/L, glucose 6.73 mmol/L, lactate dehydrogenase 77.1 U/L, adenosine deaminase 2.5 U/L, carcinoembryonic antigen negative, and no abnormality on pleural fluid culture. TB PPD was strongly positive, and T-SPOT was positive (+). On Day +290, the patient underwent PET-CT at an outside hospital, which showed: 1. Large right pleural effusion, partial compressive atelectasis of the right lung, small left pleural effusion, and small pericardial effusion. 2. Splenomegaly, splenic cyst, right renal cyst, ascites, and abdominal subcutaneous edema. 3. Postoperative changes of the left temporoparietal bone, and malacia foci in the right basal ganglia region/left temporal lobe. 4. Old TB in the right middle/upper lung. 5. Right maxillary sinusitis. 6. No obvious abnormalities in other parts of the body. The final comprehensive diagnosis at the local hospital was considered to be: 1. TB infection: tuberculous pleural effusion highly likely; 2. Diabetes mellitus, diabetic peripheral neuropathy; 3. Hypoproteinemia; 4. Pericardial effusion; 5. Peritoneal effusion; 6. Status post cerebral hemorrhage surgery. Treatment included symptomatic management with glucose lowering, albumin supplementation, diuresis, etc., and diagnostic anti-TB treatment with oral four-drug anti-TB therapy. After discharge, the patient took the four-drug anti-TB regimen regularly for more than 2 months, but his symptoms did not improve, and he gradually developed "bilateral lower extremity edema, abdominal distension, and shortness of breath," so he came to our hospital for evaluation. Since disease onset, his appetite, sleep, and energy have been poor; bowel and bladder function were acceptable; over the past 6 months, he lost about 8 kg in body weight. Past history: At age 18, he had pulmonary TB and did not receive treatment; he stated that it resolved spontaneously. Diabetes mellitus was diagnosed 2 years ago. Over the past year, he has taken dapagliflozin 1 tablet qd and metformin 0.5 g qd for glycemic control, with acceptable fasting and postprandial blood glucose control. In around Day 0, he had left temporo-occipital cerebral hemorrhage and underwent endoscopic intracerebral hematoma evacuation. After surgery, he gradually developed weakness and numbness of all four extremities, unsteady gait requiring assistance when walking, as well as slightly slurred speech and mildly slowed responses. In approximately 5 months after Day 0, gastroscopy showed positive Helicobacter pylori infection, untreated. Colonoscopy suggested colon polyps, and surgical removal was recommended, but the patient refused. On Day +235, he underwent right TAPP for a right indirect inguinal hernia, with fair postoperative recovery. He denied a history of contact with schistosomiasis-infested water; had no history of smoking or alcohol use; and denied toxic exposures. He denied a family history of hereditary disease. Physical examination after admission: Temperature 36.5℃, pulse 77/min, respiration 20/min, blood pressure 106/71 mmHg. Normally developed, poorly nourished, with an anemic appearance. Enlarged lymph nodes were present in the neck, axillae, and groin; they were relatively soft, mobile, nonadherent, and nontender, with the largest about the size of a soybean. An old surgical scar was visible in the left temporo-occipital region. The neck was supple without resistance, no jugular venous distention, no thyroid enlargement, and hepatojugular reflux was negative. The thorax showed no deformity, bilateral respiratory excursion was symmetric, breath sounds were decreased at both lower lungs, and no obvious dry or wet rales were heard. Cardiac borders were not enlarged, heart rate was 77/min, rhythm regular, heart sounds showed no obvious accentuation or diminution, and no pathologic murmur was heard in any valvular auscultation area. The abdomen was flat and soft, with no tenderness or abdominal muscle guarding throughout, no abdominal mass palpable, liver and spleen were not palpable below the costal margins, and shifting dullness was negative. Bowel sounds were normal. Mild edema was present in both lower extremities, without skin hyperpigmentation of the lower extremities. Muscle strength in all four extremities was grade IV, and muscle tone was normal.

differential_diagnoses.name: POEMS syndrome (plasma cell disorder-associated paraneoplastic syndrome)
supporting_evidence: There are progressive polyserous cavity effusions: bilateral pleural effusions, pericardial effusion, and ascites, with gradual increase.

There is clear evidence of peripheral neuropathy: weakness and numbness in both lower extremities, unsteady gait, and nerve conduction/electromyography indicates involvement of both motor and sensory nerves in all four extremities.
Endocrine abnormality present: diabetes mellitus diagnosed 2 years ago
Signs of volume overload/extravascular fluid retention: bilateral lower extremity edema, abdominal distention, shortness of breath, subcutaneous edema of the abdomen
Accompanied by splenomegaly and superficial lymphadenopathy, consistent with features of multisystem involvement
Weight loss of approximately 8 kg over the past 6 months, poor nutritional status
opposing_evidence: Phase 1 information did not provide clear evidence of monoclonal plasma cell disorder
No evidence of osteosclerotic lesions was provided in the phase I information
No hyperpigmentation of the skin of both lower extremities; no description of typical skin changes was noted in the first stage

differential_diagnoses.name: Tuberculous polyserositis (represented by tuberculous pleuritis/pericarditis/peritonitis)
supporting_evidence: History of untreated pulmonary TB at age 18; patient reports spontaneous recovery
Strongly positive PPD, positive T-SPOT (+)
PET-CT suggests old TB in the right middle/upper lung
Polyserous cavity effusions can be seen in tuberculous serositis
Chronic consumptive manifestations such as weight loss and poor appetite, sleep, and energy
opposing_evidence: Pleural fluid adenosine deaminase 2.5 U/L, low, not supportive of typical tuberculous pleural effusion
Pleural fluid culture showed no abnormality
Although pleural fluid CEA negativity is not specific, the overall pleural fluid results suggest findings between transudate and exudate, rather than a typical tuberculous exudative effusion pattern.

After more than 2 months of regular use of quadruple anti-TB therapy, the symptoms did not improve, and bilateral lower extremity edema, abdominal distention, and shortness of breath gradually developed.

differential_diagnoses.name: Pleural, pericardial, or peritoneal effusion associated with lymphoma or other malignant tumors
supporting_evidence: Over the past 6 months, body weight decreased by approximately 8 kg; poor nutritional status; anemic appearance, suggesting the possibility of a wasting disease.
Palpable lymphadenopathy in the cervical, axillary, and inguinal regions
PET-CT indicates splenomegaly
Pleural, pericardial, and peritoneal effusions are present and may be seen in malignant diseases such as lymphoma.
Pleural fluid Rivalta test positive, suggesting at least a certain exudative component
opposing_evidence: PET-CT showed no obvious abnormalities in other parts of the body.
The lymph nodes were relatively soft, had acceptable mobility, with no adhesion and no tenderness; the largest was only soybean-sized, with no obvious manifestation of a high tumor burden.

differential_diagnoses.name: Hypoproteinemia-related fluid retention/nephrotic syndrome or glomerular disease
supporting_evidence: Hypoproteinemia confirmed: total protein 57 g/L, albumin 30 g/L
Urinalysis showed urine protein 1+ and occult blood 2+, suggesting possible kidney disease.
Bilateral lower extremity edema, pleural effusion, ascites, and pericardial effusion may be caused by low colloid osmotic pressure
The pleural fluid results indicate values borderline between transudate and exudate, which is not inconsistent with an effusion caused by hypoalbuminemia.
opposing_evidence: Urine protein was only 1+; the information from the first stage showed no evidence of massive proteinuria, which is insufficient to independently explain the severe persistent progressive polyserous cavity effusions.
Accompanied by prominent peripheral neuropathy, splenomegaly, and superficial lymphadenopathy, suggesting the possible presence of a more widespread systemic disease
Pleural fluid Rivalta test positive, not a typical manifestation of a simple transudate

differential_diagnoses.name: Polyserous effusions caused by congestive heart failure or constrictive/restrictive pericardial disease
supporting_evidence: Chest tightness, shortness of breath, and bilateral lower extremity edema
Prior imaging showed mild cardiomegaly and a small amount of pericardial effusion.
Pleural effusion, ascites, and lower extremity edema may be seen in right heart dysfunction or pericardial disease.
opposing_evidence: On admission physical examination, there was no jugular venous distention, and the hepatojugular reflux sign was negative.
Cardiac borders are not enlarged, heart sounds are not significantly accentuated or diminished, and no pathologic murmurs are heard in any valvular auscultation area
The pleural effusion is not a typical simple transudate, and is accompanied by peripheral neuropathy, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, etc., which cannot be fully explained by cardiogenic factors.

differential_diagnoses.name: Systemic immune-mediated disease-associated serositis (such as systemic lupus erythematosus, IgG4-related disease, etc.)
supporting_evidence: Polyserous cavity effusions can be seen in serositis caused by systemic immune-mediated diseases
Peripheral neuropathy, hypoalbuminemia, and superficial lymphadenopathy are present, suggesting the possibility of a systemic disease.
Negative pleural fluid culture and no improvement after anti-TB treatment make a noninfectious systemic disease need to be considered.
opposing_evidence: A 53-year-old man, not part of the typical epidemiologic population for systemic lupus erythematosus
Stage 1 information did not provide typical clues suggestive of autoimmune disease, such as fever, rash, arthralgia, oral ulcers, and Raynaud phenomenon.
No evidence of autoantibodies, complement abnormalities, or IgG4-related disease was provided in Phase 1 information

recommended_exams.exam: Liver and kidney function and electrolytes
Inflammatory markers (procalcitonin, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, interleukin-6, C-reactive protein)
TB-related (interferon-gamma release assay, PPD skin test, sputum Mycobacterium tuberculosis nucleic acid test)

Rheumatology/immunology-related (ANA+ENA, vasculitis panel of six items, rheumatoid factor, complement, anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody, anti-β2-glycoprotein 1 antibody, anticardiolipin antibody, lymphocyte subsets, comprehensive immune panel)
Infectious disease panel (hepatitis B five-item panel + hepatitis C)
Pleural fluid examination (routine analysis, biochemical analysis, pleural fluid CEA, pleural fluid Gram stain, pleural fluid cytology, pleural fluid cell block)

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Further evaluation showed peripheral antecubital venous pressure of 26 cmH2O ↑, with markedly elevated antecubital venous pressure.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has chronic progressive pleural effusion, pericardial effusion, and ascites, accompanied by chest tightness, shortness of breath, and bilateral lower extremity edema. Routine echocardiography has not adequately explained the etiology, and clinically it has remained necessary to differentiate among constrictive/restrictive cardiac disease, heart failure, and simple hypoalbuminemia. Measurement of peripheral antecubital venous pressure helps determine whether venous system filling pressure is elevated and, from a hemodynamic perspective, assess whether there is impaired right heart venous return or pericardial constraint. This is helpful for explaining the mechanism of polyserous cavity effusions and peripheral edema, assessing disease severity, and deciding whether further in-depth cardiac specialty evaluation is needed.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Specialty echocardiography at the Heart Institute: thickening of the left ventricular wall, mottled hyperechoic echoes, redundancy and mild thickening of each valve with increased echogenicity, pericardial effusion (moderate), mildly elevated pulmonary artery pressure.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient presented with polyserous cavity effusions, dyspnea, and lower extremity edema. Constrictive pericarditis, heart failure, or other cardiogenic causes had been repeatedly considered earlier, but routine echocardiography showed only pericardial effusion and mild valvular regurgitation, which could not explain the persistently progressive effusions. A specialized cardiac echocardiogram was performed to further and more precisely assess myocardial, valvular, and pericardial involvement, particularly to identify clues to restrictive cardiomyopathy or infiltrative cardiomyopathy, such as ventricular wall thickening, abnormal myocardial echogenicity, valvular thickening, and changes in pulmonary artery pressure. This would not only help explain the source of the patient's volume retention and chest tightness with dyspnea, but also provide a basis for differentiating cardiac involvement related to amyloidosis, POEMS, and other conditions, and would influence subsequent treatment and risk assessment.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Skin tissue biopsy was performed; skin biopsy showed abundant eosinophilic amorphous material deposition in the subcutaneous tissue.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has multisystem involvement of unclear etiology: progressive peripheral neuropathy, weight loss, polyserous effusions, splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, diabetes mellitus, and hypoalbuminemia. Rare plasma cell-related disorders such as POEMS syndrome and amyloidosis have been included as important differential diagnoses. Skin tissue biopsy is a relatively low-risk and readily accessible method for obtaining tissue, and can directly assess for deposition of abnormal amorphous material, providing pathologic clues for determining whether systemic amyloid deposition is present, thereby helping to explain the neuropathy, cardiac manifestations, and serous cavity effusions, and providing a basis for whether to proceed with special stains and for determining the treatment direction.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: However, subsequent supplemental polarized light Congo red staining (-) did not suggest amyloidosis.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: Skin biopsy has already shown deposition of eosinophilic amorphous material, and the patient also has specialty echocardiography findings of ventricular wall thickening, speckled hyperechogenicity, and valvular thickening; clinically, it is indeed necessary to maintain a high degree of suspicion for amyloidosis, a disease that can simultaneously cause peripheral neuropathy, restrictive myocardial involvement, and fluid retention. Supplemental polarized light Congo red staining is intended to verify whether the biopsy deposits are amyloid material, directly addressing the key differential question of whether amyloidosis is present; a negative result helps exclude amyloidosis, avoid misdiagnosis, and shift the diagnostic focus to other monoclonal plasma cell-related diseases such as POEMS.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Serum immunofixation electrophoresis showed IgA λ type, M protein positive+, IgG λ type M protein positive+
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient had previously exhibited typical warning signs of POEMS, including progressive symmetric sensorimotor neuropathy, organomegaly, multiple serous cavity effusions, endocrine abnormalities, and weight loss, but previously lacked definitive evidence of a monoclonal plasma cell disorder. Immunofixation electrophoresis is more sensitive than routine protein electrophoresis and can detect trace M protein; the purpose is to determine whether a monoclonal immunoglobulin abnormality is present and to address the key diagnostic step for POEMS, multiple myeloma, MGUS, and other plasma cell disorders. The result of this test has direct value for establishing the POEMS mandatory criterion of a monoclonal plasma cell proliferative disorder and for guiding subsequent bone marrow evaluation and risk-adapted treatment.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Urine immunofixation showed positive monoclonal lambda light chain protein (+) (double bands).
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: In the setting of a high clinical suspicion for a plasma cell disorder, serum testing alone may still miss light chain-secreting clonal disease or clonal disease with low secretory burden. Although the patient has only mild proteinuria, there is hypoalbuminemia, diffuse bilateral renal parenchymal disease, and multisystem involvement; therefore, urine immunofixation can further evaluate for monoclonal light chains in the urine and determine whether a light chain-related plasma cell disorder is present. This test can both strengthen the monoclonal evidence required for POEMS and help differentiate from AL amyloidosis and other conditions, while also providing a basis for assessing renal involvement and subsequent hematologic treatment planning.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Bone marrow cytology showed active bone marrow proliferation, with the granulocytic series accounting for 57%, the erythroid series for 24%, and an increased proportion of plasma cells at 6%.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has anemia, weight loss, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, peripheral neuropathy, and urine monoclonal protein positivity, suggesting that further bone marrow evaluation is needed to confirm whether a plasma cell proliferative disorder is present. The purpose of bone marrow cytology is to assess bone marrow proliferative activity and the proportion of plasma cells, and to determine whether there is an abnormal increase in plasma cells, thereby distinguishing POEMS-associated plasma cell disorder, multiple myeloma, or other hematologic diseases. This examination is critical for confirming the underlying disease, assessing tumor burden, and formulating subsequent chemotherapy/immunomodulatory treatment plans.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Flow cytometry: P2 accounted for 0.7% of nucleated cells, expressing CD38, CD138, CD56, and clambda, without expression of CD19, CD20, CD22, or ckappa, consistent with abnormal monoclonal plasma cells.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: Although bone marrow cytology suggests an increased proportion of plasma cells, the bone marrow plasma cell burden in patients with POEMS is often not high, and morphology alone is sometimes insufficient to demonstrate clonality. Flow cytometry can further precisely define the plasma cell immunophenotype and light-chain restriction and confirm whether they are abnormal monoclonal plasma cells. For patients like this case, in whom POEMS is highly suspected clinically but differentiation from reactive plasmacytosis, MGUS, and other plasma cell disorders is required, the flow cytometry results can directly provide evidence of clonality, complete the diagnostic workup, and provide a baseline for subsequent hematology treatment selection and therapeutic response monitoring.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) testing indicated: the IGH gene was normal.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: Abnormal monoclonal plasma cells have already been confirmed in the patient. The next step is to further define their genetic characteristics to help determine the nature of the disease, differentiate it from plasma cell neoplasms such as typical multiple myeloma, and perform risk stratification. FISH testing can detect plasma cell-related genetic abnormalities that are difficult to identify on conventional karyotyping, such as IGH rearrangements. In this case, this test is performed to evaluate for high-risk genetic abnormalities while establishing POEMS-associated plasma cell disorder, thereby assisting prognostic assessment and influencing subsequent treatment intensity and regimen selection.

When there is already evidence of monoclonal plasma cells and the patient is preparing to proceed with further evaluation and treatment along the hematologic disease pathway, chromosome testing can assess, at the cytogenetic level, whether there are obvious karyotypic abnormalities, supplementing the bone marrow morphologic and flow cytometry results. The main question this test aims to address is whether this type of plasma cell abnormality is accompanied by more typical or higher-risk hematologic neoplasm-related genetic alterations, thereby helping differentiate it from other plasma cell neoplasms, assess prognostic risk, and provide a basis for subsequent treatment decisions.

The patient already had multiple clinical features of POEMS syndrome: severe peripheral neuropathy; splenomegaly and lymphadenopathy; edema manifestations such as pleural effusion, ascites, and pericardial effusion; endocrine abnormalities such as diabetes mellitus; and a monoclonal plasma cell disorder was subsequently identified. VEGF is one of the other major criteria important for POEMS and is closely related to the pathophysiology of increased vascular permeability, peripheral edema, and polyserositis with effusions. The purpose of measuring VEGF is to increase diagnostic confidence for POEMS, further distinguish it from other monoclonal plasma cell disorders and amyloidosis, and provide an objective indicator for subsequent treatment response monitoring.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Other endocrine function tests showed a slight elevation in pituitary prolactin; no obvious abnormalities were found in the remaining gonadal, thyroid, cortisol, ACTH, and other tests.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has a prior history of diabetes mellitus, and POEMS syndrome is often accompanied by multiple endocrine abnormalities; however, pre-existing diabetes alone is insufficient to fully assess the spectrum of involvement. Endocrine function testing is performed to systematically screen for involvement of the pituitary, gonadal, thyroid, and adrenal axes, and to determine the extent and severity of the endocrine abnormalities. On the one hand, this is used to satisfy the minor criteria in the diagnosis of POEMS; on the other hand, it also helps exclude other systemic diseases characterized primarily by endocrine dysfunction and edema. The test results will also affect subsequent comprehensive treatment and supportive care plans.

7.key_confirmatory_exam_information.text: Further evaluation showed peripheral antecubital venous pressure 26 cmH2O↑, with markedly elevated antecubital venous pressure. Specialty echocardiography at the cardiology institute: left ventricular wall thickening, strong speckled echoes, all valves elongated and slightly thickened with increased echogenicity, pericardial effusion (moderate), and mildly elevated pulmonary artery pressure. A skin tissue biopsy was performed; skin biopsy showed abundant eosinophilic amorphous deposits in the subcutaneous tissue, but subsequent supplemental polarized Congo red was (-), and the result was not suggestive of amyloidosis. Serum immunofixation electrophoresis showed IgA λ type, M protein positive+, IgG λ type M protein positive+, and urine immunofixation showed free light chain λ type M protein positive+ (double bands). Bone marrow cytology showed active bone marrow hyperplasia, with granulocytic series accounting for 57%, erythroid series 24%, and increased plasma cells accounting for 6%. Flow cytometry: P2 accounted for 0.7% of nucleated cells, expressing CD38, CD138, CD56, clambda, and not expressing CD19, CD20, CD22, ckappa, consistent with abnormal monoclonal plasma cells. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) indicated: IGH gene normal. Karyotype normal. Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) 234.14 pg/ml↑. On additional physical examination, hypertrichosis and leukonychia were also found. Other endocrine function tests showed mildly elevated pituitary prolactin; the remaining gonadal, thyroid, cortisol, ACTH, and other tests showed no obvious abnormalities.
